title: Enuma Elish, Tablet VII: the fifty names of Marduk
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.2, Poem of Creation (Enuma elish) (ed. A. C. Heinrich, rev. Z. J. Földi and E. Jiménez), SB VII) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: Enuma Elish (the Babylonian Poem of Creation), Tablet VII: 142 of 166 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (11 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
The gods continue to proclaim the names of Marduk with their meanings. An epilogue asks that the names be remembered, taught and pondered by later generations.

Enuma Elish ('When on high'), the Babylonian Poem of Creation, tells how Marduk, god of Babylon, defeated Tiamat, created the ordered world and became king of the gods. It was written on seven tablets and recited in Babylon during the New Year festival. The date of composition is debated (proposals range from the 18th to the 12th century BCE); the surviving copies date from the 9th to the 2nd century BCE and come from Ashur, Nineveh, Kish, Babylon, Sippar, Uruk and other sites. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/2/SB/VII) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so (BM.37379, BM.37981, BM.39798). The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the poem; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 142 of the 166 lines of the eBL edition (86%), from 11 tablets in the British Museum: K.2854 (Nineveh), K.8522 (Nineveh), K.9267 (Nineveh), K.17095 (Nineveh), BM.37379, BM.39798, K.13761 (Nineveh), BM.37981, K.12830 (Nineveh), K.18576 (Nineveh), BM.34384.

translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; * collated sign; ... broken signs of unknown number; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; <( )> sign left out on purpose by the scribe; : divider sign written on the tablet; (line break) the line runs on to the next line of the tablet; (blank space) a space left by the scribe; (gloss: ...) a note written by the scribe in small signs or in the margin.

translation.text:
1“(10) ASARI, grantor of arable land, who established irrigated fields,
2“Creator of grain and flax, who causes vegetation to spring up,
3“(11) ASARALIM, who is honored in the house of counsel, whose counsel excels,
4“The gods heed, they learn fear of him,
5“(12) ASARALIMNUNNA, the honored one, light of the father who begot [him],
6“Who implements the decrees of Anu, Enlil, Ea, (who is) Ninshiku,
7“He is their provider who assigns their portions,
8“Whose tiara increases abundance for the land.
9“(13) TUTU is [he] who effected their restoration,
10“He shall purify their shrines that they may be at rest,
11“He shall devise the magic spell that the gods may be calm,
12“Though they rise in anger, they shall turn [back].
13“He shall be supreme, alone in the assembly of the gods,
14“No one among the gods shall [make himself equal] to him.
15“Tutu they called secondly (14) ZIUKKENNA, life of the masses,
16“Who established the holy heavens for the gods,

translation.text:
17“Who took control of their courses, assigned their stations,
18“Let his deed not be forgotten among teeming humankind, let it be held fast,
19“Tutu they called thirdly (15) ZIKU, who maintains purity,
20“'God of the fair breeze, lord of obedience and consent,
21“Producer of riches and wealth, who establishes abundance,
22“Who turned all our want to plenty,
23“Whose fair breeze we caught whiff of in our great crisis,
24“Let them ever speak of his glorification, let them sing his praises!
25“Tutu let teeming humankind magnify fourthly as (16) AGAKU,
26“Lord of the sacral magic spell, reviver of the moribund,
27“Who had mercy on the vanquished gods,
28“Who removed the yoke imposed on the gods who were hostile to him,
29“Who, to free them, created humankind,
30“The merciful, whose power is to revive,
31“Word of him shall endure, not to be forgotten,
32“In the mouth of the people of this land, whom his hands have created.
33“Tutu, fifthly, is (17) TUKU, his sacral magic spell shall ever be on their lips,
34“Who with his sacral magic spell uprooted all the evil ones.
35“(18) SHAZU, who knew the hearts of the gods, who could examine their innermost,
36“Who allowed no evildoers to escape from him,
37“Who upheld the gods’ host, who contented them,
38“Who subdued the insubmissive, their (the gods’) broad [pro]tection,
39“Who administers justice, uproots twisted testimony,
40“In whose place falsehood and truth are distinguished.
41“Shazu they shall praise secondly as (19) ZISI, who silenced those who rose (against him),

146The wise and knowledgeable should ponder (them) together,
147The master should repeat, and make the pupil understand.
